newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends lower vs yen, higher vs mark in U.S..
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends lower vs yen, higher vs mark in U.S..

text.p: *Dlr ends US trading split--battered further by yen, but makes minor recovery against mark, Swiss. Late bearish talk from Conference Bd econ Fosler magnifies Japan official jawboning. *Fosler says dollar/yen 15 pct overvalued. Ford president Nasser tells RFTV dollar "only one element" impacting competitiveness. *DJIA rebounds, closes at record high, contrasts weak Nikkei.
The dollar fell against the yen Tuesday, extending overnight losses after a troika of Japanese economic leaders voiced concern over the recent dollar rally.
Late in U.S. trade, the dollar was hit by negative comments from Gail Fosler, chief economist at the Conference Board, a private economic research firm.
Fosler told an audience in Washington that the dollar was 15 percent overvalued against the yen, fueling a brief flurry of dollar selling, dealers said.
The dollar slipped to just below 115 yen on the news before bargain-hunters emerged to bolster the currency.

"The Conference Board is just an independent group, but the dollar has been trading heavily for the last couple of days, so it was poised for some retracement on a comment like that," said Russell Lascala, chief spot trader at Citibank.
The dollar closed lower at 115.23/28 yen from 115.38/48 at the open and an overnight high of 115.98. The dollar edged higher to 1.5640/45 marks from 1.5610/20 in uninspired trade.
The comments came one day after similar remarks from a Japanese finance official caused a dollar slide and reinforced perceptions that Japan may act to slow the dollar's ascent.
"It's quite clear the Japanese are trying to talk a top to the dollar right now and it's beginning to affect our markets," said Stephen Flanagan, senior foreign exchange dealer at Credit Agricole.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka at a news conference in Tokyo warned that "an excessively weak or strong yen is not favorable for the Japanese economy".
He added: "We want exchange rates to stabilize."
Later in Tokyo, top officials of Japan's Economic Planning Agency and Trade Ministry made similar statements, helping to keep the dollar on the defensive.
Heavy losses in the Japanese stock market helped offset the dollar's weakness against the yen. The Nikkei index of 225 stocks fell 2.83 percent, discouraging would-be yen buyers.
"People don't generally want to buy the currency of a country whose financial markets are getting destroyed," said Seth Garrett, director of foreign exchange at CS First Boston.
Market players also remained dubious that Japan would back up its verbal assault on the dollar with actual open market purchases of yen for dollars.
A weak yen aids Japan's global market competitiveness and Japan will not oppose a gradual dollar climb, dealers said.
"I still believe the comments out of Japan were aimed at the pace of the (dollar) move rather than the direction," Garrett said.

The dollar also got a mild boost in U.S. afternoon trading as Ford Motor Co. President Jacques Nasser downplayed the firm dollar's debilitative impact on U.S. export competitiveness in an exclusive interview with Reuters Financial Television.
"That reinforces that if there's not going to be a lot of pressure on the U.S. side (to weaken the dollar), the Japanese would like the yen to continue to weaken," Garrett said.
In other trade, sterling slipped to $1.6943/53 from $1.6950/60. The dollar rose to 1.3530/40 Swiss francs from 1.3500/10, but fell to Canadian $1.3560/65 from C$1.3614/19.
The Australian dollar rose to $0.7900/05 from $0.7886/91 at the open.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
